# Borrow one layer, not the whole

The more clearly you see a reference, the easier it is to make its remake. Every source (a designer's thinking, a real
work, a picked style) is taken apart into three layers, and only the middle one is borrowed.

| Layer | What it is | What to do with it |
|---|---|---|
| Problem | What it solves for its users | Anyone may solve the same problem |
| Mechanism | The structure that solves it: the main screen's shape, the shape the data takes, the order information arrives in, the grid's relations, one interaction | **Borrow this. That is borrowing.** |
| Expression | How it looks: palette, typefaces, shape language, illustration and icons, the copy's voice, the subject's metaphor; together, its face | **Never borrow. Grow it again from this subject, its content, its brand** |

1. **One mechanism per source**, in one sentence that carries none of its looks. "Progress is a solid bar with ticks;
   what's done is filled" is a mechanism; "yellow pills on blue" is expression. Test: give only that sentence to
   someone who never saw the original. If they could redraw the original, it is expression.
2. **Borrow across categories where you can.** A budget app borrowing a tide app's curve, a recipe app borrowing a
   camera's dial: the result doesn't look like either. Excellent work in the same category shows the floor and what to
   avoid. The medium still stays the same (an app from an app, a page from a page).
3. **The most visible spot is the subject's own**: something only this subject has (the card's "form from content"),
   not the borrowed mechanism. The mechanism is the bones; the subject is the face. Crossing two sources' mechanisms,
   or letting a mechanism meet an image from the subject, beats borrowing one alone.
4. **The remake test**, after building: take `screenshot` of yours and of the reference at the same width, look at
   the two one after the other, and ignore every word on both. Would someone who knows the original call yours
   its new version? Then keep the mechanism and redo the expression (colours, shapes, type). Also check the borrowed
   mechanism actually arrived. A pixel diff doesn't answer this (a different ground colour alone pulls the numbers
   apart): the eye decides.
5. **Say the source.** On the card, and in one sentence when showing the person: whose what was borrowed. What you can
   say out loud is borrowing; what you would hide is copying.
